guards.rule: none

Built-in kitchen appliances (stove, fridge, oven) that are part of a kitchen counter run must be rendered as visible objects in the scene, even if they are integrated into the counter module. The build stage should not skip them as 'built_in' without providing a visible representation.

Furniture strokes on the 'tefriş' layer that form recognizable shapes (sofa, chairs, table) must be read as furniture pieces even if they are not explicitly labeled. The reading stage should use shape recognition to identify common furniture items from stroke patterns.
A bathroom set is incomplete without a mirror over its washbasin; the set's completeness check must list a mirror as a required partner of the basin, not only the basin, toilet and tub.
A room under 3 m2 with no door of its own and no fixtures is a passage or shaft, not a room; the reading must type it hall or shaft, not 'other', and the model must not build it as an enclosed room.

A kitchen run is not assembled until its sink, hob and worktop are visible as a working set; the group's completeness check must verify the sink and stove are fitted to the counter, not only present in the piece list.

A salon with a dining zone in its program must have its dining set (table and chairs) placed as a coherent group; the reading must not merge the dining zone label into the living room without placing the dining furniture.
A children's room with one child must have one bed, not two; a second double bed in a single-child room is a misread and must be retyped to a single bed or removed.
A small interior room (under 4 m2) with a shoe cabinet and no entrance door is a storage or utility space, not a hall; the reading must type it storage, not hall.
A veranda or balcony drawn in the plans must be built as a distinct site area with a floor, posts and railing; the site stage must not skip it because it has no outline in the model data.
A balcony drawn in the plans must be built as a distinct site area with a floor and railing; the site stage must not skip it because it has no outline in the model data.

The building's coordinate frame must be anchored to the sheets' outline corner, not to the outer wall faces of a reference region; the reading stage must re-anchor the frame so that all regions and coordinates are consistent with the sheets.
The ground floor's level mark in the section must be read as the building's z=0, not as +0.50; the reading stage must re-baseline the level frame so that all relative marks are correct.
A zone label (e.g. 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ') inside a room is a sub-zone of that room, not a second room; the reading must not treat it as a separate label that causes a 'more labels' warning.
A door whose approach is blocked by furniture (no free passage) is a misread; the reading must check the approach and re-read it as a window if it is not a passage.
A gap in the outer wall whose approach is blocked by furniture (no free passage) is a misread; the reading must check the approach and re-read it as a window if it is not a passage.
A warning that an opening is 'no passage' because furniture blocks its approach is a fit finding, not a reading error; do not apply door_to_window to an opening already read as a window.
A wide outer-wall opening (>= 1.5 m) in a bedroom or living room that is blocked by furniture and has no clear passage function should be read as a window, not a door.
A narrow outer-wall opening (< 0.80 m) that is completely blocked by furniture and has no passage function should be read as a window, not a door.
A wide outer-wall opening (>= 1.5 m) in a bedroom that is blocked by furniture and has no clear passage function should be read as a window, not a door.
Furniture must not cover or block windows; if a piece is placed in front of a window, it should be moved to a free spot in the room.
If the big loop stops with 0 cycles and a low score, the agent should be given another round to attempt improvements.
If multiple views are marked for review, the agent should be given another round to address them.

When a dining group cannot be placed in a living room due to walkway constraints from a door, the solver should allow placement in a corner or along a wall that does not block the walkway, or the door position should be adjusted if it is a reading error.
When a kitchen run is missing essential appliances (fridge, hob), the solver should add them to the run if there is space, or the room layout should be adjusted to accommodate them.

When a bed blocks a door and cannot be moved due to overlap or room constraints, the door position should be adjusted if it is a reading error, or the bed should be resized to a smaller model that fits.
Dressing rooms should have a styled floor (rug) and baseboards to match the project's style.
Outdoor views should have a believable environment, not low-poly placeholders.
Child's bedrooms should have playful decor (bunk bed, climbing equipment, colorful mural) to match the reference.
Bathroom renders should have warm wood, textured stone, and functional styling (mirror, towel rail) to match the project's style.
A bathroom set (bathroom_set group) must always include a mirror over the washbasin; the set is incomplete without it.
A kitchen or dining room with a reference style that includes wall art must have at least one wall art piece placed on a visible wall.
A kitchen island or counter that is a standalone piece (not part of a kitchen_run with sink/stove) must have a sink or cooktop fixture on its worktop to look functional.
A living room with a reference style that includes plants must have at least one potted_plant placed in a visible corner or beside the seating group.

A room's furniture must be one coherent set: the agent picks models from a single style family and adds the soft styling layers (textiles, decor) the reference shows, so a room never reads as a catalog of clashing pieces.
A dining table's base must be a finished, coherent model that matches the room's style, never a low-poly placeholder that reads as a rendering error.
A bathroom's main camera must frame the room's main pieces (basin, toilet, bath/shower), not a bare corner.
A bathroom's styling set includes a mirror over the basin plus the soft layers (towels, decor, warm light); the agent adds them when the reference shows them.
A room's furniture and styling must match its named brief (a children's room is playful and layered, not a generic adult bedroom); the agent restyles when the render misses the brief.
Every furnished room gets its styled surfaces (rug, art, cushions, small objects on surfaces); the agent adds them so no room reads as a bare shell.
A room's furniture must be one coherent set: a desk's model must coordinate with the bed, dresser and wardrobe, not an off-style industrial piece.
Furniture surfaces in a client-ready render are styled with small objects (books, decor, a lamp); the agent adds them so no surface reads as bare.
A room's furniture must match its named brief; a children's room is furnished as a children's room (playful, multi-level), not as a generic adult bedroom.
A bedroom holds one coherent bed set; the agent resolves duplicate or mismatched beds and styles the room to its brief.
A bedroom holds one coherent bed set; a second, differently-styled bed in the same room is a mismatched set the agent must resolve.
A room's palette and styling must match its named brief; a children's room is colorful and playful, not sterile adult neutrals.
A bathroom's main camera must frame the room's main pieces (shower, toilet, basin), not a blank wall or corner.
A camera's focus must be the room's main group, not a blank wall with the main piece cut off.
A wet room's lighting is warm and ambient, not flat clinical white; the agent sets the lighting to match the reference.
A room's lighting fixtures must fit its palette and provide warm ambient light; a loud artificial object that clashes with the scheme is restyled by the agent.

The furniture library must include organic/boho armchair models (rattan, boucle, curved wood) so that a room styled organic/boho is not forced to take a mid-century modern piece; a style tag that is not present in the library must not be assigned to a room.
Exterior presentation views must be rendered with the project's facade materials, roof detailing, and site landscaping applied, not as a grey-box massing study.
Exterior renders must include exterior lighting (bollards, architectural lights) to match the reference standard; a completely dark exterior is not client-ready.
Exterior renders must include designed landscaping (planters, paths, hardscape) rather than a flat, untextured green ground plane.
Exterior facade renders must show rich material contrast (timber, stone, dark metal) and a designed entrance, not a flat white box.
Exterior cameras must be at eye level (1.5-1.7 m) or above the ridge, never a top-down aerial that crops the house to a fragment of roof.
Exterior renders must convey the project's style (modern, warm, layered) with proper materiality and landscape, not as a grey-box massing study with crude lollipop trees.
The house's entrance door must be a library entrance door (statement door), not a generic door; the build stage must assign the correct door family by role.

Decor items that cannot rest on their host due to minor penetration (host pokes through cloth) are acceptable to leave unbuilt if the penetration is small and the decor is not critical to the room's function.

Decor items (cushions) that cannot rest on their host due to angle-dependent penetration are acceptable to leave unbuilt if the penetration is small and the decor is not critical to the room's function.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece (e.g., a bed) but is named by an AI pass as a distinct type (e.g., floor_lamp) that fits its size should be built as that type, not left out as a detail.
The reading stage must read all entity types in the source DWG file, including ATTDEF (attribute definitions), to ensure no data is lost.
Site decor items read outside the walls of a level (e.g., L1) that repeat the ground plan's symbols at the same place should be used for the ground floor (L0) site, not left unused.
When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms (e.g., 'Salon' and 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ'), the reading stage must split the room into two distinct rooms, not treat the second label as a duplicate.
Printed area labels (e.g., '9,00 m²' of 'HOL' on L1) must be used for area checks of the corresponding space, not left unused.
When walls are drawn as face lines, the reading stage must use all wall primitives, not just those on the chosen layer (e.g., 'SIVA'), to ensure no walls are left out.
Site decor read on an upper level that duplicates the ground-floor plan at the same coordinates is a reading artifact, not a missing site element; the site stage takes the ground-floor set.
A drawing layer of pure line entities that no stage uses and no warning names is a reading artifact, not a missing model element.
A drawn bookshelf that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.

A drawn potted plant that is not built because its assigned model was removed by audit is rebuilt by swapping to a real library model of the same type (never a generated model when a real product fits).
A drawn dining table that is not built because its assigned model fails the fit rules is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type that passes the fit rules.
A drawn chair that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.
A drawn shoe cabinet in a hall that is not built is rebuilt by the furniture agent fitting a library shoe cabinet of the drawn size.
A drawn desk that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.
A drawn office chair that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.
A drawn desk in a room that is not built is rebuilt by the furniture agent fitting a library desk of the drawn size.
A drawn console table that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.

A drawn piece in a bedroom that is 4.64 m long and 0.68 m deep and typed 'unknown' is a misread of a built-in wall unit or long low cabinet; the reading stage should type it from its size and room context, or the building stage should treat it as a wall element, not a furniture item.

A drawn piece in a hall that is 0.50 m long and 0.12 m deep and typed 'unknown' is a misread of a small wall element (e.g. a coat hook, a small shelf, or a door stop); the reading stage should type it from its size and room context, or the building stage should treat it as a wall element, not a furniture item.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading stage should detect the internal wall that separates the two labelled spaces and split the room outline accordingly, rather than keeping the larger label and losing the smaller room.
When no library model of a building's window or door family fits an opening's dimensions, the parametric opening in the style's finish is the correct fallback and is not a defect.
When no library model of a building's door family fits an opening's configuration (e.g., double leaf), the parametric door in the style's finish is the correct fallback and is not a defect.

When a fixture is built with a parametric mesh due to a library gap, and a suitable library model exists that fits the drawn size and room, the fitting stage should select the library model to ensure higher quality and consistency.

When a piece is built with a parametric mesh due to a library gap, and a suitable library model exists that fits the drawn size and room, the fitting stage should select the library model to ensure higher quality and consistency.
The furniture agent should ensure that large blank walls in living areas are styled with art or other decor to create a layered, inhabited look, as expected in photorealistic renders.
The furniture agent should ensure that key surfaces like coffee tables are styled with small decor objects to make the space feel inhabited and complete.
The furniture agent should ensure that windows are treated with curtains or other softening elements to match the project's style and create a cohesive look.
When a piece's style clashes with the room's atmosphere, the fitting stage should select a library model that better matches the project's style and reference.
The furniture agent should ensure that beds are dressed with layered, textured bedding to match the project's style and create a cohesive, inhabited look.
A nightstand (or any small side table) is complete on its own; do not flag a missing decorative object on it as a defect.
Interior doors must carry a finished, textured wood look that matches the project's reference style, never a plain untextured panel.
The main entrance must be defined with an approach (steps or a ramp) and a focal point, not left as a bare door in a wall.
Every exterior door that is an entry must be framed with an approach (steps or a ramp), not left as a bare door.
A room's camera must frame the room's main piece; a view that shows an empty corner while the room's anchor piece is out of frame is a defect.
A drawn desk that the decor stage placed must survive the agent stage; dropping it is a loss, not a choice.
An opening read from the drawing (with evidence) must be built; dropping it in the build stage is a loss.
Structural grid bubbles (axis labels) on the 'AKS YAZI' layer are drawing annotations and are correctly not built.
Decor items drawn on a host piece that is itself not built are correctly not built.
A cushion, pillow or detail drawn on a piece is a detail of that piece, not a piece of its own, and is correctly not built separately.
Decor that would stand in front of a window and reach over its sill, or that has no free spot on the worktop, is correctly not built.
Structural grid bubbles (axis labels) on the 'AKS' layer are drawing annotations and are correctly not built.
Columns drawn on the 'KOLON' layer are structural annotations and are correctly not built as furniture.
Level mark symbols on the 'kot' layer are drawing annotations and are correctly not built.
An exterior label whose surface is already built from site.paving / parking / grass is correctly not built as a separate element.

Every outdoor space named in the documents (veranda, balcony, terrace) must be given a built outline (floor slab and edge) at the site stage, even when it is not a labelled room, so that its drawn edges, steps and guard can be built and attached.

When a drawn furniture label (e.g., 'SIFONIYER') is present in the documents but no corresponding piece is built, and the nearest valid placement is more than 1 m from the label, the system should either (a) place the piece at the nearest valid location and flag the discrepancy for architect review, or (b) omit the piece and flag the label as unfulfilled. The current behavior of silently omitting the piece without a clear flag is not acceptable.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished with its defining set (bench, full-length mirror, open storage or hanger rail); a lone wardrobe is not a dressing room and the room's program must be completed, not just re-modelled.
An interior camera must frame the room's layout and its main pieces, not be pressed against a door leaf or furniture edge at a low angle.
An exterior view must frame the main facade, entrance and the house's scale at eye level (1.5-1.7 m), not a corner of the roof and a hedge from too high and too far.
A scene check failure (S2) on a level means the build stage left a geometry inconsistency; the build stage must be re-run for that level.
A scene check failure (S3) on a level means the build stage left a geometry inconsistency; the build stage must be re-run for that level.
A furniture piece present in the decor stage must not be silently dropped by the agent stage; if the agent removes or moves it, the record must name it.
A stove that is built into a kitchen counter run (a hob in the worktop) is part of the counter module and does not need a separate scene object; the conservation check must not flag it as missing.

A fridge that is built into a kitchen counter run (an integrated fridge in the run's fronts) is part of the counter module and does not need a separate scene object; the conservation check must not flag it as missing.
An exterior view that must show a window must frame the facade section containing that window; the camera position and target must be chosen so the window is in frame.

Drawings on the furniture layer ('tefriş') that depict a sofa or chairs around a table must be read as furniture pieces (sofa, chairs, table) and placed in the model; strokes on the furniture layer that no piece uses are lost furniture.

When the documents name a space (e.g. 'ANTRE') that is a second label of an existing room outline, the reading stage must split the room outline into two rooms if the documents show a wall or clear boundary between them; otherwise the space is lost.
A piece named in the documents (e.g. '*SIFONIYER' for a dresser) must be placed in the model at or near its named location; the furniture agent must add it if the reading did not.
A kitchen counter shown in the plan must be built in the model; if the kitchen run is incomplete, the furniture agent must complete it with the missing counter segments.

A drawn kitchen counter that the fit stage left unbuilt because it cut a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the kitchen run is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the counter is built, not dropped.

A standard bedroom-set piece (nightstand) that is left unbuilt because it cuts a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the sleeping group is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the nightstand is built, not dropped for a spatial conflict.

A decoration whose host piece is not built is a cascading loss: the build stage must either build the host (re-solving its group) or explicitly remove the decoration, never leave it dangling as 'not built'.
A labelled outdoor space (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a bounded site area with its own floor and guard, not left as ad-hoc geometry with no outline.

A room's main group (dining table and its chairs) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main group is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A room's main piece (a hall's console table) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main piece is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A ray through a window opening must not hit furniture: the build stage must clear any piece that blocks the way through an opening.
A bathroom washbasin must be part of a complete bathroom set (basin, mirror, vanity or at least a mirror above it); a bare bowl with no mirror is a fundamental design failure.
A bathroom's washbasin must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the bathroom but misses the basin is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A bathroom washbasin must be part of a complete bathroom set (basin, mirror, vanity or at least a mirror above it); a basin with no mirror over it is a fundamental design failure.
A small enclosed room (under 3 m2) with no function, no pieces and no door of its own is most likely a misread: it is a hall or passage, not a room of its own, and must be typed accordingly.
A sliding door read from lines in an outer wall that is blocked by furniture across its approach and has no outside destination is a misread window: convert it to a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall that is blocked by furniture across its approach and has no outside destination is a misread window: convert it to a window at the floor's sill.
Furniture that covers a window opening must be moved to a free place in its room, clear of the opening.
Views marked for review must be re-evaluated in the next agent round after fixes are applied.

When a room's dining set is drawn but the solver cannot place it due to walkway constraints from doors, the drawn pieces should be kept as drawn and the walkway constraint should be relaxed for the dining zone, or the dining table should be moved to a position that satisfies both the walkway and the room's program.

When a kitchen's run is drawn but the solver cannot complete it due to missing appliances (fridge, hob), the drawn kitchen run should be kept as drawn and the missing appliances should be added as separate pieces, or the kitchen run should be re-solved with the missing appliances included.

When a bed_double blocks a door and cannot be moved due to overlap or plausibility constraints, the bed should be swapped for a smaller model (bed_single or a smaller bed_double) that fits the room and does not block the door, or the door should be moved to a different wall.
Every room must have a visible floor finish that matches the project's style.
The outdoor view through windows must show a believable environment with trees, ground cover, and site elements, not a low-poly placeholder.
A child's room must have wall art (murals, posters, or art) to match the reference style.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood, textured stone, and functional styling (mirror, towel rail) to match the project's style.
A bathroom must have a mirror over the basin to match the reference style.
A bathtub's model must match the project's light, minimalist aesthetic.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood textures, a vanity unit, a mirror, and a towel rail to match the project's style.
Kitchen renders must show styling and 'lived-in' layers to match the reference, not a raw architectural model.

A room typed as a child's room must be furnished with a cohesive, age-appropriate set (playful, warm, child-sized); a generic adult office or minimalist set is a mismatch that the furniture agent must resolve by swapping the models to a matching style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a generic adult bedroom is a failure of the furniture set, not the camera.
A modern white office chair is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate chair that matches the room's style.
A minimalist white-framed office desk is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate desk that matches the room's style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a cluttered adult bedroom with clashing furniture is a failure of the furniture set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a wall showing a bare corner is a bad camera.
A nightstand in a master bedroom must match the room's warm, organic style; a loud, artificial object (e.g. a neon lamp) that clashes with the natural wood and neutral palette is a mismatch.
An armchair in a master bedroom must match the room's organic, boho style; a mid-century modern piece that clashes with the natural wood elements is a mismatch.
A render of a master bedroom must show a warm, organic, and layered interior; a sterile, unfinished shell with clashing surfaces is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A master bedroom must be lit with warm, cozy light; a flat, cool ambient light that feels like a hospital ward is a failure of the lighting and material set.
A render of a hall must show a warm, textured, and functionally styled interior; a bare, empty shell with no console table or decor is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A hall must have styled surfaces (console table, decor, and a rug); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a door leaf is a bad camera.
A storage room must have styled surfaces (hanging clothes, a mirror, etc.); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A bedroom under 12 m2 that the solver cannot relayout still gets one potted_plant in a corner the solver leaves free, so the room is never rendered bare.
When the current bed model is a blocky placeholder and a generated model of the same type and style is available, swap to the generated model rather than leaving the placeholder.
A bedroom render that shows only blocky furniture and flat walls is a fit failure: the furniture agent must add at least one plant, one textile and one wall item before the view is scored.
An interior camera that frames only a door and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A dressing room with only a wardrobe is missing its program: the furniture agent must add a mirror, a bench and wall art so the room reads as a dressing room, not a storage closet.
A room whose walls are completely bare in the render is missing the wall-art layer: the furniture agent must add at least one framed piece on a free wall span.
An interior camera that frames only a wall corner and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A facade that renders as a flat white box is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look (wood, stone, or brick) that matches the project's reference style.
A ground-floor plinth with no planters, shrubs or ground cover is a site failure: the site must include planters and a hedge or fence to soften the transition to the lawn.
A facade that renders as a bare clay model is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A facade that renders as a flat untextured white surface is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
An exterior wall with no place to sit is a site failure: the site must include a patio set or bench to make the exterior feel lived-in.
An exterior wall with no lanterns, wall sconces or path lights is a site failure: the site must include exterior lighting to define the space at night.
A facade that renders as a grey-box massing study is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A house with outside doors but no library entrance door is a build failure: the build stage must assign a statement entrance door model to the entrance opening.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a chair in the salon) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a shoe cabinet in the hall) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a desk in the room) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (an office chair in the room) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (an unknown item in the hall) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must split the outline at the wall between them (a wall not read) so each label keeps its own room; the label with the largest printed area is kept only as a fallback.
A room's furniture must read as a designed space, not a collection of pieces; the furniture stage must keep the room's function clear (a bedroom is not an office).
A piece must look like its type in every view; the fit stage must choose a model whose silhouette matches the type (a bed_double must not read as a bed_single).
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position.
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place and match its drawn size; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position and size.
A dressing room (Soyunma Odası) must contain at least a mirror and a bench or seating in addition to a wardrobe to be functionally complete; a single wardrobe is insufficient for the room type.

When a drawn furniture label (e.g., 'SIFONIYER' for dresser) is present in the documents but no corresponding drawn piece is found within 1 m of the label, the system should attempt to place the furniture at the label's location if the space is free, or flag it for manual review if the space is obstructed.

Elevation checks must be able to run even if the north arrow is missing, by using the plan's orientation or a default bearing, or by flagging the missing north arrow as a critical error that blocks the check.

When a drawn section does not align one-to-one with the plan (e.g., due to roof overhangs or section cuts), the check should either adjust the comparison to account for the offset or flag the misalignment for manual review.
guards.target: the drawn section r# is not checked point by point against the roof

guards.rule: Elevations must have a view bearing or side assigned to them to allow comparison with the model; if missing, the system should infer the bearing from the plan or flag the elevation as incomplete.

When an interior door is drawn as a double and the library holds no double-leaf model, build it parametric in the style's finish and record a library_gap; do not force a single-leaf model onto a double opening.

A piece whose room is None (orphaned, not assigned to a room) cannot be refitted or swapped; the fitting stage must assign every placed piece to a room before the library-quality check, or the check must skip orphaned pieces instead of flagging them.

When two interior doors in the same tight space (hall, corridor) are built from the same heavy traditional model, the fitting stage should vary at least one to a lighter or different-style model from the library to avoid a dated, repetitive look.

When an opening is read twice (duplicate evidence) and is wide (>= 1.8 m), the build stage must build it as a single opening (or a double door) rather than dropping it; duplicate reads of the same opening should be merged, not discarded.

When a host piece is not built (e.g., removed or not placed), its attached decor elements should either be re-parented to a valid host or built independently if they are standalone items; the build stage should not silently drop decor just because its host is missing.
When a section prints a floor level offset from the plan's 0.00 datum, treat the plan's 0.00 as the finished-floor reference and ignore the section's offset for level assignment.
Small drawn pieces adjacent to level-mark text are symbols, not furniture; move them to the symbol layer.
Furniture name texts in the drawing confirm the presence of the named piece; no action needed if the piece is already built.
Zone labels in the drawing confirm the presence of the named zone; no action needed if the zone's furniture is already built.
Small seat-sized pieces adjacent to a dining table are chairs; type them by context.
When an armchair's inferred front is blocked by a door or wall, and no alternative orientation is free, keep the inferred front.
When an armchair's inferred front is blocked and no alternative model fits, keep the inferred front.
When an armchair's inferred front is blocked and no alternative orientation is free, keep the inferred front.

When a furniture name text in the drawing names a piece that is not drawn at that location, and the nearest valid place is more than 1 m away, add the piece at the text's location if it fits the room's program, or flag it for review if it does not.
When a door in the outer wall is blocked by a drawn piece, and the piece is not a door or a window, read the opening as a window at the floor's sill height.
An outer-wall opening whose approach is fully blocked by a drawn counter or fixture is a window, not a door: the reading must classify it by what stands in front of it, not by its width.
A wall unit must not stand over a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the unit to a free wall span.
A piece must not cover a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the piece to a free spot.
A labelled outdoor area (veranda, terrace, balcony) in the plan must be built as a distinct site element with a floor slab and railing/outline, not left as an unrecognised open space.
A room typed as 'hall' with an area less than 3 m2 and no circulation function should be re-typed as 'storage' or 'other'.
Stairs should not be assigned to a kitchen room; they belong in a hall, stairwell, or circulation space.
A labelled veranda, terrace or balcony in the site plan must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, floor and railing, not dropped as 'no outline'.
A living room with a seating group must include a rug under the coffee table and sofa.
A bathroom with a washbasin must include a mirror above it.
Site areas labeled as 'BALKON' or 'VERANDA' in the plan must be built as functional outdoor rooms with floors, guards on open edges, and roofs where indicated, not left as unbuilt outlines.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or wet room must be paired with a mirror (over or beside it) as part of the bathroom set; a basin without a mirror is an incomplete set.
Every kitchen worktop must carry a few real small appliances and decor pieces (kettle, toaster/coffee machine, board, fruit bowl), placed off the hob, sink and window.
A drawn terrace/balcony site area must be built as a slab with a guard before any door is allowed to open onto it; a door whose opening has no built deck is a defect.
A terrace must be built and reachable from outside before a drawn window is promoted to a terrace door; an un-built deck with a door on it is a defect.
An upper-floor opening that reaches a terrace must have a built deck and a guard; an un-built deck behind a door is a fall hazard.
An outside door must open onto a built, reachable deck or ground; a door whose target terrace is not built is an 'entrance to a window' defect.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or kitchen must carry a mirror mounted over or beside it; a basin left against a bare wall is incomplete.

When a site area (veranda, balcony, terrace) is drawn with a roof or eaves in the plan, the building stage must construct that roof slab and its supports; a columned outdoor space without its drawn roof is a loss, not a valid omission.

Outdoor-space columns must be sized to a slender structural proportion (not thick piers), and any balcony/veranda drawn with an adjacent sloped roof must have that sloped roof built, not a flat slab on heavy columns.

Every outside door that meets a level difference must be served by a designed entrance: solid-tread steps with cheek walls and a landing (or a ramp where accessibility asks), never a bare concrete stair with a thin handrail.
Every garden step must sit on its riser and the ground and be finished in the house's base stone or render with a coping; bare concrete treads in the grass are not acceptable.
Each outdoor floor must carry the material of its use (terrace, steps, path, drive) in one language with the house's base, never one bare slab everywhere.
Every outdoor room must be dressed for outside: no rug or carpet on its floor and only furniture made for outside (no upholstered indoor sofa or indoor table/chair).

rules_proposed.rule: Dressing rooms should have a styled floor (rug) and baseboards to match the project's style.
Outdoor views should have a believable environment, not low-poly placeholders.
Child's bedrooms should have playful decor (bunk bed, climbing equipment, colorful mural) to match the reference.
Bathroom renders should have warm wood, textured stone, and functional styling (mirror, towel rail) to match the project's style.
A bathroom set (bathroom_set group) must always include a mirror over the washbasin; the set is incomplete without it.
A kitchen or dining room with a reference style that includes wall art must have at least one wall art piece placed on a visible wall.
A kitchen island or counter that is a standalone piece (not part of a kitchen_run with sink/stove) must have a sink or cooktop fixture on its worktop to look functional.
A living room with a reference style that includes plants must have at least one potted_plant placed in a visible corner or beside the seating group.

A room's furniture must be one coherent set: the agent picks models from a single style family and adds the soft styling layers (textiles, decor) the reference shows, so a room never reads as a catalog of clashing pieces.
A dining table's base must be a finished, coherent model that matches the room's style, never a low-poly placeholder that reads as a rendering error.
A bathroom's main camera must frame the room's main pieces (basin, toilet, bath/shower), not a bare corner.
A bathroom's styling set includes a mirror over the basin plus the soft layers (towels, decor, warm light); the agent adds them when the reference shows them.
A room's furniture and styling must match its named brief (a children's room is playful and layered, not a generic adult bedroom); the agent restyles when the render misses the brief.
Every furnished room gets its styled surfaces (rug, art, cushions, small objects on surfaces); the agent adds them so no room reads as a bare shell.
A room's furniture must be one coherent set: a desk's model must coordinate with the bed, dresser and wardrobe, not an off-style industrial piece.
Furniture surfaces in a client-ready render are styled with small objects (books, decor, a lamp); the agent adds them so no surface reads as bare.
A room's furniture must match its named brief; a children's room is furnished as a children's room (playful, multi-level), not as a generic adult bedroom.
A bedroom holds one coherent bed set; the agent resolves duplicate or mismatched beds and styles the room to its brief.
A bedroom holds one coherent bed set; a second, differently-styled bed in the same room is a mismatched set the agent must resolve.
A room's palette and styling must match its named brief; a children's room is colorful and playful, not sterile adult neutrals.
A bathroom's main camera must frame the room's main pieces (shower, toilet, basin), not a blank wall or corner.
A camera's focus must be the room's main group, not a blank wall with the main piece cut off.
A wet room's lighting is warm and ambient, not flat clinical white; the agent sets the lighting to match the reference.
A room's lighting fixtures must fit its palette and provide warm ambient light; a loud artificial object that clashes with the scheme is restyled by the agent.

The furniture library must include organic/boho armchair models (rattan, boucle, curved wood) so that a room styled organic/boho is not forced to take a mid-century modern piece; a style tag that is not present in the library must not be assigned to a room.
Exterior presentation views must be rendered with the project's facade materials, roof detailing, and site landscaping applied, not as a grey-box massing study.
Exterior renders must include exterior lighting (bollards, architectural lights) to match the reference standard; a completely dark exterior is not client-ready.
Exterior renders must include designed landscaping (planters, paths, hardscape) rather than a flat, untextured green ground plane.
Exterior facade renders must show rich material contrast (timber, stone, dark metal) and a designed entrance, not a flat white box.
Exterior cameras must be at eye level (1.5-1.7 m) or above the ridge, never a top-down aerial that crops the house to a fragment of roof.
Exterior renders must convey the project's style (modern, warm, layered) with proper materiality and landscape, not as a grey-box massing study with crude lollipop trees.
The house's entrance door must be a library entrance door (statement door), not a generic door; the build stage must assign the correct door family by role.
When no library model of a building's window or door family fits an opening's dimensions, the parametric opening in the style's finish is the correct fallback and is not a defect.
When no library model of a building's door family fits an opening's configuration (e.g., double leaf), the parametric door in the style's finish is the correct fallback and is not a defect.

When a fixture is built with a parametric mesh due to a library gap, and a suitable library model exists that fits the drawn size and room, the fitting stage should select the library model to ensure higher quality and consistency.

When a piece is built with a parametric mesh due to a library gap, and a suitable library model exists that fits the drawn size and room, the fitting stage should select the library model to ensure higher quality and consistency.
The furniture agent should ensure that large blank walls in living areas are styled with art or other decor to create a layered, inhabited look, as expected in photorealistic renders.
The furniture agent should ensure that key surfaces like coffee tables are styled with small decor objects to make the space feel inhabited and complete.
The furniture agent should ensure that windows are treated with curtains or other softening elements to match the project's style and create a cohesive look.
When a piece's style clashes with the room's atmosphere, the fitting stage should select a library model that better matches the project's style and reference.
The furniture agent should ensure that beds are dressed with layered, textured bedding to match the project's style and create a cohesive, inhabited look.
A nightstand (or any small side table) is complete on its own; do not flag a missing decorative object on it as a defect.
Interior doors must carry a finished, textured wood look that matches the project's reference style, never a plain untextured panel.
The main entrance must be defined with an approach (steps or a ramp) and a focal point, not left as a bare door in a wall.
Every exterior door that is an entry must be framed with an approach (steps or a ramp), not left as a bare door.
An interior camera must frame the room's layout and its main pieces, not be pressed against a door leaf or furniture edge at a low angle.
An exterior view must frame the main facade, entrance and the house's scale at eye level (1.5-1.7 m), not a corner of the roof and a hedge from too high and too far.
Every room must have a visible floor finish that matches the project's style.
The outdoor view through windows must show a believable environment with trees, ground cover, and site elements, not a low-poly placeholder.
A child's room must have wall art (murals, posters, or art) to match the reference style.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood, textured stone, and functional styling (mirror, towel rail) to match the project's style.
A bathroom must have a mirror over the basin to match the reference style.
A bathtub's model must match the project's light, minimalist aesthetic.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood textures, a vanity unit, a mirror, and a towel rail to match the project's style.
Kitchen renders must show styling and 'lived-in' layers to match the reference, not a raw architectural model.

A room typed as a child's room must be furnished with a cohesive, age-appropriate set (playful, warm, child-sized); a generic adult office or minimalist set is a mismatch that the furniture agent must resolve by swapping the models to a matching style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a generic adult bedroom is a failure of the furniture set, not the camera.
A modern white office chair is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate chair that matches the room's style.
A minimalist white-framed office desk is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate desk that matches the room's style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a cluttered adult bedroom with clashing furniture is a failure of the furniture set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a wall showing a bare corner is a bad camera.
A nightstand in a master bedroom must match the room's warm, organic style; a loud, artificial object (e.g. a neon lamp) that clashes with the natural wood and neutral palette is a mismatch.
An armchair in a master bedroom must match the room's organic, boho style; a mid-century modern piece that clashes with the natural wood elements is a mismatch.
A render of a master bedroom must show a warm, organic, and layered interior; a sterile, unfinished shell with clashing surfaces is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A master bedroom must be lit with warm, cozy light; a flat, cool ambient light that feels like a hospital ward is a failure of the lighting and material set.
A render of a hall must show a warm, textured, and functionally styled interior; a bare, empty shell with no console table or decor is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A hall must have styled surfaces (console table, decor, and a rug); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a door leaf is a bad camera.
A storage room must have styled surfaces (hanging clothes, a mirror, etc.); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A bedroom under 12 m2 that the solver cannot relayout still gets one potted_plant in a corner the solver leaves free, so the room is never rendered bare.
When the current bed model is a blocky placeholder and a generated model of the same type and style is available, swap to the generated model rather than leaving the placeholder.
A bedroom render that shows only blocky furniture and flat walls is a fit failure: the furniture agent must add at least one plant, one textile and one wall item before the view is scored.
An interior camera that frames only a door and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A dressing room with only a wardrobe is missing its program: the furniture agent must add a mirror, a bench and wall art so the room reads as a dressing room, not a storage closet.
A room whose walls are completely bare in the render is missing the wall-art layer: the furniture agent must add at least one framed piece on a free wall span.
An interior camera that frames only a wall corner and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A facade that renders as a flat white box is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look (wood, stone, or brick) that matches the project's reference style.
A ground-floor plinth with no planters, shrubs or ground cover is a site failure: the site must include planters and a hedge or fence to soften the transition to the lawn.
A facade that renders as a bare clay model is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A facade that renders as a flat untextured white surface is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
An exterior wall with no place to sit is a site failure: the site must include a patio set or bench to make the exterior feel lived-in.
An exterior wall with no lanterns, wall sconces or path lights is a site failure: the site must include exterior lighting to define the space at night.
A facade that renders as a grey-box massing study is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A house with outside doors but no library entrance door is a build failure: the build stage must assign a statement entrance door model to the entrance opening.

When an interior door is drawn as a double and the library holds no double-leaf model, build it parametric in the style's finish and record a library_gap; do not force a single-leaf model onto a double opening.

A piece whose room is None (orphaned, not assigned to a room) cannot be refitted or swapped; the fitting stage must assign every placed piece to a room before the library-quality check, or the check must skip orphaned pieces instead of flagging them.

When two interior doors in the same tight space (hall, corridor) are built from the same heavy traditional model, the fitting stage should vary at least one to a lighter or different-style model from the library to avoid a dated, repetitive look.

rules_proposed.rule: none

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading stage should detect the internal wall that separates the two labelled spaces and split the room outline accordingly, rather than keeping the larger label and losing the smaller room.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished with its defining set (bench, full-length mirror, open storage or hanger rail); a lone wardrobe is not a dressing room and the room's program must be completed, not just re-modelled.

A room's main group (dining table and its chairs) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main group is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A room's main piece (a hall's console table) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main piece is a camera failure, not a model failure.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must split the outline at the wall between them (a wall not read) so each label keeps its own room; the label with the largest printed area is kept only as a fallback.
A room's furniture must read as a designed space, not a collection of pieces; the furniture stage must keep the room's function clear (a bedroom is not an office).
A piece must look like its type in every view; the fit stage must choose a model whose silhouette matches the type (a bed_double must not read as a bed_single).
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position.
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place and match its drawn size; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position and size.
An outer-wall opening whose approach is fully blocked by a drawn counter or fixture is a window, not a door: the reading must classify it by what stands in front of it, not by its width.
A wall unit must not stand over a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the unit to a free wall span.
A piece must not cover a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the piece to a free spot.

prevention.what: something the documents or an earlier stage hold is missing from the model (a labelled veranda, drawn site symbols, a room, an opening, a piece)

rules_proposed.rule: Built-in kitchen appliances (stove, fridge, oven) that are part of a kitchen counter run must be rendered as visible objects in the scene, even if they are integrated into the counter module. The build stage should not skip them as 'built_in' without providing a visible representation.

Furniture strokes on the 'tefriş' layer that form recognizable shapes (sofa, chairs, table) must be read as furniture pieces even if they are not explicitly labeled. The reading stage should use shape recognition to identify common furniture items from stroke patterns.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece (e.g., a bed) but is named by an AI pass as a distinct type (e.g., floor_lamp) that fits its size should be built as that type, not left out as a detail.
The reading stage must read all entity types in the source DWG file, including ATTDEF (attribute definitions), to ensure no data is lost.
Site decor items read outside the walls of a level (e.g., L1) that repeat the ground plan's symbols at the same place should be used for the ground floor (L0) site, not left unused.
When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms (e.g., 'Salon' and 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ'), the reading stage must split the room into two distinct rooms, not treat the second label as a duplicate.
Printed area labels (e.g., '9,00 m²' of 'HOL' on L1) must be used for area checks of the corresponding space, not left unused.
When walls are drawn as face lines, the reading stage must use all wall primitives, not just those on the chosen layer (e.g., 'SIVA'), to ensure no walls are left out.
Site decor read on an upper level that duplicates the ground-floor plan at the same coordinates is a reading artifact, not a missing site element; the site stage takes the ground-floor set.
A drawing layer of pure line entities that no stage uses and no warning names is a reading artifact, not a missing model element.
A drawn bookshelf that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.

A drawn potted plant that is not built because its assigned model was removed by audit is rebuilt by swapping to a real library model of the same type (never a generated model when a real product fits).
A drawn dining table that is not built because its assigned model fails the fit rules is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type that passes the fit rules.
A drawn chair that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.
A drawn shoe cabinet in a hall that is not built is rebuilt by the furniture agent fitting a library shoe cabinet of the drawn size.
A drawn desk that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.
A drawn office chair that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.
A drawn desk in a room that is not built is rebuilt by the furniture agent fitting a library desk of the drawn size.
A drawn console table that is not built because its assigned model is unusable is rebuilt by swapping to a library model of the same type and size.

A drawn piece in a bedroom that is 4.64 m long and 0.68 m deep and typed 'unknown' is a misread of a built-in wall unit or long low cabinet; the reading stage should type it from its size and room context, or the building stage should treat it as a wall element, not a furniture item.

A drawn piece in a hall that is 0.50 m long and 0.12 m deep and typed 'unknown' is a misread of a small wall element (e.g. a coat hook, a small shelf, or a door stop); the reading stage should type it from its size and room context, or the building stage should treat it as a wall element, not a furniture item.
A room's camera must frame the room's main piece; a view that shows an empty corner while the room's anchor piece is out of frame is a defect.
A drawn desk that the decor stage placed must survive the agent stage; dropping it is a loss, not a choice.
An opening read from the drawing (with evidence) must be built; dropping it in the build stage is a loss.
Structural grid bubbles (axis labels) on the 'AKS YAZI' layer are drawing annotations and are correctly not built.
Decor items drawn on a host piece that is itself not built are correctly not built.
A cushion, pillow or detail drawn on a piece is a detail of that piece, not a piece of its own, and is correctly not built separately.
Decor that would stand in front of a window and reach over its sill, or that has no free spot on the worktop, is correctly not built.
Structural grid bubbles (axis labels) on the 'AKS' layer are drawing annotations and are correctly not built.
Columns drawn on the 'KOLON' layer are structural annotations and are correctly not built as furniture.
Level mark symbols on the 'kot' layer are drawing annotations and are correctly not built.
An exterior label whose surface is already built from site.paving / parking / grass is correctly not built as a separate element.

Every outdoor space named in the documents (veranda, balcony, terrace) must be given a built outline (floor slab and edge) at the site stage, even when it is not a labelled room, so that its drawn edges, steps and guard can be built and attached.
A furniture piece present in the decor stage must not be silently dropped by the agent stage; if the agent removes or moves it, the record must name it.
A stove that is built into a kitchen counter run (a hob in the worktop) is part of the counter module and does not need a separate scene object; the conservation check must not flag it as missing.

A fridge that is built into a kitchen counter run (an integrated fridge in the run's fronts) is part of the counter module and does not need a separate scene object; the conservation check must not flag it as missing.
An exterior view that must show a window must frame the facade section containing that window; the camera position and target must be chosen so the window is in frame.

Drawings on the furniture layer ('tefriş') that depict a sofa or chairs around a table must be read as furniture pieces (sofa, chairs, table) and placed in the model; strokes on the furniture layer that no piece uses are lost furniture.

When the documents name a space (e.g. 'ANTRE') that is a second label of an existing room outline, the reading stage must split the room outline into two rooms if the documents show a wall or clear boundary between them; otherwise the space is lost.
A piece named in the documents (e.g. '*SIFONIYER' for a dresser) must be placed in the model at or near its named location; the furniture agent must add it if the reading did not.
A kitchen counter shown in the plan must be built in the model; if the kitchen run is incomplete, the furniture agent must complete it with the missing counter segments.

A drawn kitchen counter that the fit stage left unbuilt because it cut a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the kitchen run is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the counter is built, not dropped.

A standard bedroom-set piece (nightstand) that is left unbuilt because it cuts a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the sleeping group is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the nightstand is built, not dropped for a spatial conflict.

A decoration whose host piece is not built is a cascading loss: the build stage must either build the host (re-solving its group) or explicitly remove the decoration, never leave it dangling as 'not built'.
A labelled outdoor space (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a bounded site area with its own floor and guard, not left as ad-hoc geometry with no outline.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a chair in the salon) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a shoe cabinet in the hall) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a desk in the room) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (an office chair in the room) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (an unknown item in the hall) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.

When an opening is read twice (duplicate evidence) and is wide (>= 1.8 m), the build stage must build it as a single opening (or a double door) rather than dropping it; duplicate reads of the same opening should be merged, not discarded.
